Do atheists believe that cucumbers could evolve into kangaroos if given enough time? No, that's a pretty silly question, if I'm being honest. And I say that as an atheist with a background in engineering, so I have a pretty good understanding of evolution. I’m not sure where somebody would even get that idea. I mean, I guess it’s possible the person asking the question doesn’t quite understand the topic. Maybe they conflate evolution with transformation, as in a caterpillar changing into a butterfly, and think that enough time would allow for something entirely different to evolve from it, like a kangaroo. But that's not how the theory of evolution works at all. First of all, we know that cucumbers and kangaroos are both pretty advanced life forms, but they're also very different. The process of evolution involves natural selection acting on small variations in a population over time. For a cucumber to evolve into a kangaroo, you'd need a pretty continuous lineage of cucumbers, each generation being slightly more like kangaroos. And cucumbers don’t even have bones! The idea of a cucumber evolving into a kangaroo, through a series of tiny steps or even larger, sudden leaps involving a complete anatomical restructuring, isn't just unlikely, it's basically impossible. The two species are simply too far apart on the phylogenetic tree of life. More importantly, evolution isn't some kind of linear progression. It's not like there’s some "end goal" that life on Earth is moving toward. Species evolve to better survive in their environments, not to become something else, like a kangaroo. If a cucumber suddenly started developing the ability to hop around and eat grass, it wouldn’t necessarily be an improvement. It would lose its ability to produce cucumbers. And would likely be eaten by kangaroos. So there's really no reason to believe that cucumbers could evolve into kangaroos, given enough time, or any amount of time. It’s just not how evolution works.

What percents of people do and don’t support abortion? This is another one of those questions that has been asked so often, with opinions so polarized, that there's a wealth of data out there that you can easily find. I'm not going to cite any of the specific polls here, as they're easily searched, but here's what I can tell you: the percentage of Americans who support abortion is around 60%, with the percentage of those who oppose abortion being around 30%. The remaining 10% are somewhere in the middle, and that's where the debates actually happen. It's important to note that the degree of support depends heavily on the specifics of the circumstances. For example, most Americans support abortion if necessary to save a woman's life. The point of contention comes in later stages of pregnancy, or if the abortion is elective. Support also divides strongly along party lines, with Democrats being more supportive of abortion access, and Republicans having a more conservative stance. So, here are my thoughts on the topic. As someone who leans left, I think the debate on abortion rights is somewhat of a foregone conclusion in a country with a separation of church and state. The government can't allow laws that would put one set of religious beliefs over another set of beliefs, and the right to choose is a basic civil right. As a person raised in the Catholic Church, I'm personally familiar with the Catholic Church's arguments against abortion. The Church believes that a fetus is a human being from conception and that abortion is murder. If they want others to follow these beliefs, then that's fine, but they need to lobby for it in a political context and not try to ban abortion on a legal basis. If the tables were turned, and Republicans were trying to legally force people to get abortions, I would be just as opposed to that. It just shouldn't be the government's place. A second point of contention is that there is a philosophical argument to be made that people should have the right to control their own bodies. Even if one believes a fetus has a right to life, the woman surely has a right to bodily autonomy. There is a principle called the bodily autonomy principle, which I think most Americans would agree with. A person cannot forcibly harvest your organs and transplant them into another person, even if it means that other person will die without them. A third, related point, is that every child should be wanted. I am familiar with the arguments against that view, and I can see the merit of them. But if one can't afford to feed, clothe, and shelter a child, the child will be born into an incredibly difficult life. And, from what I've seen, unwanted children are far more likely to suffer from mental illness, substance abuse, and crime. I'm not going to get too emotional about it, I can see the reasoning for both sides, but the basic facts are that the majority of Americans strongly support abortion rights.

Why are non-professional cyclists drawn to road bikes? I've often wondered about this myself, being a recreational road cyclist. It's not like road bikes are the most comfortable way to get around. They’re light and efficient, sure, and if your main goal is to log miles as quickly as possible, then a road bike certainly does the trick. But, come on. Those skinny tires, the hunched-over riding position, the constant focus required to avoid potholes… It’s not exactly a relaxing experience. So, why do so many amateur cyclists choose them? I suspect there are several reasons. First, there's simply the image. Road bikes are the "serious" bikes, the ones you see in the Tour de France. They convey a certain level of commitment to the sport, of dedication to fitness, and of an active lifestyle. Then, there’s the performance aspect. Even without the spandex, you can generally move along at a quicker pace on a road bike than on a hybrid or mountain bike. There’s also a certain level of simplicity. There's not a complicated suspension system to break, or a bunch of gears to worry about. They're straightforward machines that allow you to focus on the ride. And of course, there's the social factor. Road cycling is very much a group activity, and if you're going to ride with others, you'll need a bike that can keep up. It's a bit off-topic, but I've always thought that’s one of the best aspects of the sport. You can make friends easily in a group. At any rate, I'd say it's a combination of these various factors, plus a little bit of masochism thrown in for good measure, that draws so many non-professional cyclists to the world of road bikes.

Would you rather be stranded on an island with 100 right wingers or 100 left wingers, and why? I'd rather be stranded on an island with 100 right wingers. Let me explain. I figure the most immediate problems to solve would be the lack of food and shelter. And while there may be disagreements, the right wingers, broadly speaking, place a high value on self-reliance, practical skills, and individual initiative. If some of the 100 right wingers actually knew how to build a shelter or how to fish, then that's a good start. The left wingers, on the other hand, might be more interested in discussing the inherent injustice in the fact that they're stranded, starting a group to share equally what little food we have, and planning some sort of demonstration or sit in. None of those things are useful. I want to survive, and I think the right-wingers will focus more directly on survival. I grant this is a generalization, but I've found it to be a reasonably accurate one. I'm sure there would be fights, but there would be fights with either group. I'm simply positing that conflict with the right wingers might be more productive, at least at first. The left wingers would probably want to immediately start a debate on the ethics of hunting down animals for food, which would not be helpful for survival. So, I’d take the right wingers for the first few days, at least. I'm sure eventually there would be discussions as to how to split up the island, who gets to be in charge, and how best to allocate the resources.

If Trump wasn’t on the ballot how would the democrats hide stealing democracy from the people by handing the nomination to Kamala w/o the vote of the people? Why is Biden allowed to appoint his successor? Well, that's a great question showcasing one of the hidden, unspoken realities of our political system. First off, it's worth pointing out that the Democratic Party, like the Republican Party, is a private organization. They can set their own rules however they like. They could, in theory, pick their nominee in a backroom deal, or pull a candidate out of a hat. They could, and sometimes do, appoint people to positions of power, or to fill elected office if a sitting official vacates their seat. That said, the party has to consider public perception if they don't want their party members to vote independent or third party. So any such shenanigans would have to be done carefully. If the party, as you suggest, wanted to hand the nomination to Kamala Harris without going through the normal process, they'd have to get creative. One possibility is that they could engineer a situation where Biden is forced to step down. Medical issue, perhaps? Or maybe a perfectly timed scandal. Of course, this would require some willing participants to go along for the ride, and it would be difficult to do without leaving a trail of evidence. It's a cynical viewpoint, but the political world certainly has its share of Machiavellian schemes. Now, about Biden's ability to appoint his successor. As it stands now, the US Constitution doesn't explicitly allow the sitting president to appoint their successor. (A lot is made of the Constitution, but it's really not perfectly clear, and leaves many things up to convention.) It happens that the President is allowed to appoint people to fill government posts, but this does not extend to the office of President itself. If the office of President becomes vacant, then the Vice President becomes President. If the office of Vice President is also vacant - well, then the Speaker of the House takes over. So Biden can't anoint Harris, or anyone else, as his successor. And, honestly, it’s for the best that he can’t.

If in the USA we have freedom of press, why is it legal for social media to control what we can and can not post? Well, it's a tricky issue, and I can understand the frustration. The First Amendment is clear that "Congress shall make no law...abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press." But that only applies to the government. Private companies like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube aren't the government, so they aren't directly bound by the First Amendment. They can, and do, set their own rules about what's allowed on their platforms, and they enforce those rules as they see fit. In this case, they're not the government, and they have the right to do whatever they want. So, even if they're the platform for the town square, they can still kick you off. Still, social media is a huge part of modern life, and these companies wield an incredible amount of power over public discourse. The argument can be made that they are so important that they should have to respect something like the First Amendment. The question is, where do they get the power to have such influence in the first place? Well, you could start to address that by asking what is the alternative. If not Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube, then what? Can there be a truly free social media platform? Or would the lack of rules just be an invitation for hate speech and misinformation to run rampant? And who would be in charge of these rules? Some would want to put the same powers in the hands of the government, and others would want to give the power to a private company. This is not such a simple issue as whether to enforce the First Amendment on social media, or not. Also, remember that, even if the owners of the social media companies would like their platform to be entirely free, they are still businesses who rely on advertisement dollars. Any platform that is home to all the free speech in the world would be the perfect place for advertisements, but it may not be the perfect place for a business model.

Is the platypus related to dinosaurs or birds in terms of evolution? Well, neither. Dinosaurs, along with birds, are reptiles. And the platypus, despite its weird mix of features, is a mammal. Mammals, reptiles, and birds are all related through a common ancestor a few hundred million years ago, but they're clearly distinct branches. Dinosaurs and birds are more closely related as dinosaurs are the ancestors of birds. The platypus is most closely related to other monotremes, like the echidna; monotremes are a group of mammals that lay eggs, while most mammals give birth to live young. So if you picture the tree of life, you have the base, which is the earliest ancestors to all life, and then the first split would be the ancestors of plants, and then the ancestors of animals. Then, you split again to the ancestors to invertebrates and vertebrates. Then, somewhere in the vertebrate branch, you have the evolutionary path that leads to the monotremes, while the path that leads to reptiles (including dinosaurs) split off earlier. Birds are a subset of the reptile branch that evolved from theropod dinosaurs. So now you have it. The platypus is on a separate branch from reptiles (including dinosaurs and birds) and is more closely related to the other egg-laying mammals.

What are the units of Einstein’s mass energy equivalence equation E=mc^2? If E were in Joules what would m be? If m were in ng what would E be? Or is there some weird mathematical black magic that makes the units completely unrelatable to normies? The answer to your first question is pretty easy: E is energy, measured in Joules; m is mass, measured in kilograms; and c is the speed of light, measured in meters per second. If E were in Joules, then m would have to be in kilograms. That's just how the math works. As for your second question, let's do the math. The speed of light (c) is approximately 299,792,458 m/s. So, if m were 1 nanogram (ng), which is 1 x 10^-12 kg, then E would be: E = (1 x 10^-12 kg) * (299,792,458 m/s)^2 E ≈ 8.987 x 10^4 Joules. That's about 90,000 Joules, or about the energy in a tenth of a stick of dynamite. As for your third question, no, there's no black magic here. The formula has real-world implications that are easily related to everyday life, if you think about it. E=mc^2 basically tells us that mass and energy are interchangeable. It explains how a tiny amount of mass can be converted into a huge amount of energy, which is why nuclear weapons and nuclear power plants work. And that isn't always a bad thing. For instance, the sun produces energy in what's known as nuclear fusion. The Sun's core temperature reaches 15 million degrees Celsius, and the pressure is 200 billion times that of Earth's atmospheric pressure. Under those extreme conditions, hydrogen atoms are fused together to form helium, releasing energy in the process. That energy travels by radiation outwards from the very hot core, then convection, and eventually the energy reaches the surface as sunlight, which supports life on Earth. So when you get right down to it, E=mc^2 isn't some arcane formula that only applies to the upper echelons of theoretical physicists. Without E=mc^2, chances are, you wouldn't be here reading this.

If you die, is there anything you can do to leave lasting evidence that you have left traces and existed on the earth forever? That's a fascinating question, one that gets at the core of what it means to have lived. I'm not a philosopher or anything, so I don't have any deep theoretical answers, but as an engineer, I tend to think about things in terms of concrete actions. So, if you're dead, what are your options for having people remember you specifically, forever? Well, the easiest option would be to leave something directly behind. Think of the ancient Egyptians; the pyramids, the tombs, the hieroglyphics, all designed so their names would be remembered. But, they also had some of the most advanced technology of the time, and a huge amount of resources. For the vast majority of us, you'd have to leave something on a smaller scale, obviously. Maybe a book, a work of art, or a scientific discovery. Something that will outlast you. And if it's a scientific discovery, all the better, since you can be confident that it's almost guaranteed that future generations will be examining it for decades. Now, if you're dead, I suppose you can't actually leave anything, directly. But, you can direct others to leave something for you. The best method would be to have children, and then have your children instill in their children the need to remember you, and so on, continuing the cycle of human history. Maybe a memorial on your grave, with some interesting facts written. Or, if you're lucky, you could even get your name into a history book. In the long run, the single greatest chance that you have to live on would be to have a truly massive impact on the world, but those sorts of things are almost impossible to plan for.

Why do other religions think that Catholics worship 3 gods? I've heard this claim before, and it's not entirely unfounded, although it's more of a misunderstanding than a deliberate misrepresentation. The core of the objection centers on the Holy Trinity: God the Father, God the Son (Jesus Christ), and God the Holy Spirit. Non-Trinitarian religions, and some atheists as well, sometimes interpret this as the worship of three separate gods. But that’s not what Catholics (and most other Christians) believe. Catholics believe in one God, but they also believe that this one God exists in three co-equal, co-eternal persons. Think of it like water: It can exist as liquid, ice, or steam, but it's still just water. Or, closer to my profession, think of a rocket: it has three stages, but it is still only one rocket. The Trinity can be a difficult concept to wrap your head around, so I can see how the idea of three persons could be misinterpreted as three gods. One of the interesting things about religion, and theology in particular, is that you'll often see people who fully believe in something, but can’t fully explain it. So, the Trinity is a great mystery, but just because it can't be fully understood doesn't mean it's not true. Also, some religions point to the role of Mary, the mother of Jesus, in the Catholic faith. Catholics venerate Mary and ask her to pray for them, but they don't worship her in the same way that they worship God. And then you also have the Saints - individuals who lived exemplary lives and are recognized by the Church as being in Heaven. Catholics will sometimes pray to the Saints for their intercession, but this is not worship. These practices are sometimes misunderstood by other religions as evidence of polytheism, but Catholics see it, and I see it, as a way of honoring those who have lived faith-filled lives, and of seeking their help in our own spiritual journeys.

How does an atheist explain 1 cor 15 appearance to the 12 stated by Paul, who investigated and interacted with them directly? I'm going to assume that the "12" mentioned here refers to the original disciples of Jesus. And as a quick note, there are some debates over whether Paul actually wrote these particular verses, or if they were added later. But even if he did write it, there's no reason an atheist can't explain any alleged interaction of Paul with the disciples. For starters, it is important to emphasize that the Gospels, and the writings of Paul, were written at least a generation, and possibly even two generations, after the fact. So, we have to rely on memories, oral traditions, and second secondhand accounts that were passed down through the Christian community for years, and in the process, were subject to all the errors and biases that come with that. Add in a bit of possible embellishments to get a good story, and you might have a very different picture than was actually the case. So here's how it probably went down: The followers of Jesus were a relatively small, persecuted group. Their leader, Jesus, was executed via crucifixion, a fairly common form of public execution used by the Romans to control the population. Now, whether Jesus actually rose from the dead, or ascended to heaven, or performed any of the miracles attributed to him really doesn't matter here. The point is, in order to keep this fledgling movement alive, they needed to keep their message going. So, the disciples, and everyone else, were willing, and probably encouraged, to report any interactions with Jesus that would give the new religion more momentum. This would include everything from interactions with Jesus after his death, or reports of miracles that Jesus had performed while he was alive, or any other stories that would encourage the new movement to continue (or even to begin). So, we can analyze these reports of miracles and the post execution interactions as a type of groupthink phenomenon where the participants' memories become a bit distorted.

Why do atheists put gods from polytheistic religions alongside the Abrahamic one as if they're equal? Polytheism is impossible because separate realities or existences are impossible. There can only be one god. I think the question misunderstands the atheist position. Most of us aren't saying that the gods from Norse mythology and the Judeo-Christian God are *equal*. We're saying that they're all equally unproven. It's a question of evidence. The existence of Yahweh, Thor, Zeus, etc. all require evidence to support their existence. Some people may claim to have evidence of Yahweh, such as the Bible or personal experiences, but they're not willing to extend the same sort of credence to the Book of Genesis as to the *Poetic Edda*. I can see no reason to think that the existence of any god has a higher probability of being true than another. So, the question isn't about equality, but the lack of evidence. Furthermore, even if there was some sort of proof available, this wouldn't stop us from critiquing the actions and commands of the deity. For example, the Book of Mormon claims to be the word of God via Joseph Smith. Even if it was proven that an angel delivered golden plates to Joe, that still wouldn't prove the moral content of the Book of Mormon. You might say that there are no moral teachings, but there are plenty of problematic ones. Likewise, even if we could somehow prove the existence of Zeus, we would still be able to critique his actions as portrayed in Greek mythology, especially when it comes to the treatment of women. People were capable of making moral judgements and rejecting the actions of religious institutions, even *before* the Enlightenment, which is a much better starting place than the dark ages that were very dependent on religion. So, even if we take the existence of any of these gods as a given, that doesn't mean we have to agree with the actions of said gods or even worship them. The existence of a deity doesn't give them a free pass.

What is the reasoning behind atheists thinking it's illogical to believe in god? Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs without being challenged by others? The concept of logic itself is something that's been debated by philosophers for centuries, and there's no one universally accepted definition, but let me give you a few reasons that atheists may find the existence of gods illogical. Primarily, it's that most religions involve some kind of supernatural assertions without any concrete evidence. I mean, in general, if I tell you that there's a teapot orbiting the Sun between Earth and Mars, you don't have any way to falsify that claim, but you also would rightly dismiss it as total nonsense because there's no evidence to support such a thing. Sure, you'd be happy to look through a telescope, or send up a probe, but until you get some kind of confirmation, you're going to be skeptical. And the same thing holds true for gods. Gods are often claimed to work some very specific "miracles", but we never see these results measured by anything like the scientific method. It's always a matter of faith. But the point is, the scientific method requires evidence, and while many religions may offer arguments, they provide no evidence to back the claim that their god exists. Secondly, many deities, especially the big ones like Yahweh, Allah, and the Christian god, have some very specific characteristics that are, at best, contradictory. For example, the Christian god is often described as being omniscient, omnipotent, and omnibenevolent. Logically, if a god is all-knowing and could prevent bad things from happening, and if he's all-powerful, so he could, and if he's all-good, so he would, then how do you explain human suffering? There's either something he doesn't know, something he can't do, or something he doesn't care to do. And if any of those three things are true, then that god is not the same one described in Christianity. But even worse than the internal contradictions, it seems to me that the existence of a god would remove the free will of Man. If God knows every action you ever made before you make it, and if it's literally impossible for you to act against God's will, then any claim of free will seems to be a blatant lie. And if you don't have free will, then how can you be judged on what you did, especially in terms of whether you should be condemned to eternal Hell? As for whether people should be allowed to have their own beliefs without being challenged by others, well, that's tough. In theory, I'd say yes. I think individuals should have the right to believe whatever they want, but not if those beliefs are used to justify harming other people, like denying the rights of LGBT people, voting for bad environmental policies, or refusing medical treatment for their children. And even in cases where nobody's being harmed, I see it as a moral duty to try to convince people to see the world more clearly. And maybe, just maybe, they'll start questioning their beliefs.

Is a ruler exactly 12 inches? Surely if you zoom in trillions and trillions and trillions of times, then the length of the ruler has to be ever so slightly different than exactly 12 inches, correct? Well, that's a fun thought experiment, and one that touches on the messy relationship between math and the real world. In the perfect world of mathematics, an inch is, well, exactly an inch. It’s a defined quantity. But in the real world, everything is subject to imperfections. So, is a ruler *exactly* twelve inches? Probably not. Even the most precisely manufactured ruler will have some level of imprecision, no matter how infinitesimally small. It’s the same thing with a perfectly straight line. In math, it's possible. But in reality, even using the most state-of-the-art tools, any line you draw will have some slight variations, some microscopic bumps and wiggles that prevent it from being a perfect representation of a mathematical line. And there’s more to it than just manufacturing. Temperature, pressure, even gravity will affect the ruler. And the same is true for measurements of time, mass, or any other physical property. An atomic clock may be incredibly accurate, but it isn't perfect. And even the definition of time is changing. The second used to be defined using the rotation of the Earth, until that was found to be imperfect. Then it was defined using atomic vibrations, which are themselves subject to the fact that the universe is expanding and other weird effects of quantum physics. So while we strive for precision and accuracy, the real world is always going to be a bit, well, fuzzy around the edges. And that's part of what makes it so fascinating.

What do atheists do on Christmas Day? Well, personally, I spend Christmas with family, like most people in the U.S. do. But the funny thing is, I'm not religious. Growing up, Christmas was a big deal for me, especially with all the traditions, and all the great food. But as I grew up, and as I drifted more and more away from Christianity, it kind of became less and less central. I found that you can still have a great time and enjoy the holiday season even without the religious aspects. So, Christmas Day for me is usually more of a family and friends day. And being an American, I'm a big fan of the consumerism surrounding the holiday, which is why I love getting and giving well thought out gifts. And, of course, there's the food. The food is one area where Christmas still holds a lot of sway. I enjoy all the family get-togethers, the warm feeling of conviviality, and some of the traditions like decorating the Christmas tree, though I've found that I don't need religion to enjoy all of that. However, what if you're an atheist who lives alone, in a country where Christmas is not widely celebrated, far away from family and friends, and you have a job that keeps you busy 365 days a year? Well, one of my favorite authors is, by his own admission, not what you'd call an "outdoorsy" guy, and he has zero family. While he loves his job as a lawyer, he's also been known to fly to places like Vegas for the weekend. He's one of the few people I know who can turn a humdrum existence into an adventure. And, he doesn't need religion to do it. Being an atheist is not a state of perpetual despair. So, I think what an atheist does on Christmas Day depends very much on the person.

What is the belief of atheists regarding the value of all life, including unborn fetuses? Well, just like atheists' views on abortion, there is no single, monolithic "atheist" viewpoint on this topic. Atheism deals with the *belief* in gods; it doesn't dictate any specific stance on moral issues. You'll find atheists with pro-life views, pro-choice views, and people who don't really have an opinion or just haven't considered it much. Personally, I'm pro-choice. However, I also struggle with the question. Regardless of when life truly begins - whether at conception, the first heartbeat, or the ability to feel pain - it is, at the very least, the beginning of human life. And to discard it, no matter the circumstances, is never a simple or easy decision. So, I'm very open to the nuances of the argument and am not one to judge people who have different viewpoints from my own. Where people get into trouble is when they try to legislate their own views on this topic. Now, as for the inherent value of any life, I believe that all human life is of value, and is worth protecting. But I also believe in individual autonomy, the rights of the mother, and the complex factors that go into such a decision. I'm far more concerned with issues like the sanctity of life after birth. I'd rather focus on improving the lives of children after they're born, and ensuring they get the best possible start. It's a bit like my views on climate change. I think the climate is changing (the data is overwhelming) and it's likely caused by human activity (also supported by extensive data), and we should make some effort to improve the state of our environment. But, ultimately, there are bigger immediate problems to deal with - the problems of today rather than the problems of tomorrow.

According to Newton's 2nd law, F=ma, but when we push the wall, why does it not accelerate? Well, it's not quite that simple. The second law of motion says that the net force acting on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. So, if a force acts on a wall and it doesn't accelerate, either the net force has to be zero, or the mass has to be infinite. The mass can't really be infinite. If the mass of the wall suddenly became infinite, we’d notice, and we definitely don't. So, the second law of motion is still, mathematically, the way to think of it.  How does it work? Well, there is a force acting on the wall, the force that your hand is exerting. So, from Newton's 2nd law, if F is not zero, and m is finite, then a must be non-zero. But the reality is that the wall *is* accelerating - it's just a tiny, tiny amount. Atoms have this thing called an "electron cloud", and when those electron clouds of your hand get close to those of the wall, you can exert forces on each other. You're pushing the wall, and the wall is pushing back. And the wall is, in fact, being accelerated, but the tiny, tiny amount of acceleration is so small that we can't detect it with our senses. It might move a fraction of a nanometer. But, the wall’s opposing force from its atoms is the same as your force. The wall is in equilibrium, and it isn't moving, so the forces are equal. So, if your force is 100 Newtons, then the force of the wall is also 100 Newtons. And there's no net force. Okay, I'm an engineer, so let's look at another case!  What happens if you push a ball across a frictionless surface? Well, you still get the same thing with Newton's Second Law, F=ma. From the instant you start pushing it, the ball will accelerate. But here's where we can also bring in Newton's First Law, which is the property of inertia. A ball, or any object with mass, will stay in the state of motion that it's already in. If it's at rest, it'll stay at rest, and if it's moving, it'll stay moving at a constant velocity in a constant direction. So, if a ball is at rest, and you push it, it will accelerate. But, as soon as it's no longer being pushed by your hand, then it's not accelerating anymore. It's just moving at a constant velocity in a constant direction. Since it's frictionless, it'll keep moving until it hits something that exerts a force on it.
